records.name: Seoul
records.current_summary:
The capital's courts have been the country's clearest rights forum for trans people: a ruling finalised in July 2024 held that police who told a transgender person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while had infringed personal rights, calling comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right and awarding damages. A 2021 national human-rights-commission survey (591 trans respondents) quantified the underlying fear: 41% had used a restroom of another gender out of fear of mistreatment, 39% restricted food and drink to avoid public restrooms, 36% went without; a 2021 district-court judgment awarded damages against a beauty academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.

Recognition has also liberalised judicially: a May 2024 regional decision approved gender-marker change for five trans people without surgery, holding that a surgery requirement violates bodily integrity and reducing the old surgical prerequisites to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them.
records.current_localsOnly: School facilities are resident/student-facing: binary school restrooms leave 69% of trans students surveyed (86 respondents) uncomfortable, with documented patterns of avoiding water and leaving school early to avoid outing, and 39% mistreatment reported in a Busan-area study (208 respondents); legislative advocacy for gender-neutral single-occupant restrooms and inclusive school rules concerns the domestic school system, which foreign visitors do not enter.

sources.claim: Seoul-specific ruling coverage (Korea Times, 22 July 2024): the Seoul Central District Court (presiding judge Chung In-jae) dismissed the state's appeal and ruled partially for plaintiff A in a damages lawsuit against the state, awarding 300,000 won (about $240) of the 3 million won claimed; the decision became final on 2 July 2024 after neither party appealed, holding that a police officer's advice to an LGBT person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed personal rights — "the right to comfortably use restrooms is a fundamental and universal human right." Underpinning data: a 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 trans respondents found 41% used another-gender restrooms out of fear of mistreatment, 39% avoided food and drink, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether; the piece also cites a 2021 Pohang branch of the Daegu District Court ruling of 7 million won damages against an academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.

National judicial-framework item (Yonhap, 8 May 2024): the regional court in the central county of Yeongdong approved male-to-female gender-marker change for five transgender people without sex reassignment surgery, holding it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that every human being has the right to live according to one's gender identity; the national court guidelines that previously required surgery have been downgraded to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them. The ruling is not from a capital court — it evidences the national judicial trend the record cites for Seoul, and no Seoul-specific source covers that claim.

records.name: Quintana Roo
records.current_summary: Quintana Roo: worse than national for what a visitor actually meets — the country's main tourist corridor, with a documented policing problem. The Cancún/Riviera Maya hotel zone is a massive international tourism envelope with a commercially gay-friendly surface, but municipal and state police have been repeatedly documented committing discriminatory acts against LGBT+ people, with multiple recorded assaults during detention concentrated in Tulum and Playa del Carmen; the community describes officers as untrained in human-rights standards. The municipal Directorate for Sexual Diversity recorded three formal discrimination complaints in a single year, including violence against a transgender woman, and two Tourist Police members were fired after their own body cameras showed them running an extortion ring against visitors with portable card terminals. Cancún's immigration detention facility is documented as a place of systematic rights violations with no accountability — relevant to a visitor whose documents are questioned. Countervailing: the state enacted legal gender recognition in 2020 and banned conversion practices in December 2023. Scored relative to the national score (0.55) for Mexico.
records.current_localsOnly: Quintana Roo's 2020 legal gender recognition procedure and its December 2023 ban on conversion practices are resident-facing; neither changes the exposure of a visitor.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch feature (31 March 2025), 'Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges'. Country-wide survey of legal gender recognition: 22 of 32 states had legislated an LGR procedure by March 2025, while six states (Aguascalientes, Chiapas, Durango, Querétaro, Tabasco, Tamaulipas) had reformed nothing, leaving trans people's documents permanently mismatched; also documents coercive detention and border scrutiny risks for document-mismatched travellers.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mexico - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ rights in Mexico' page gives the state-level legal picture a Quintana Roo visitor stands under: same-sex marriage has been permitted in the state since 2012 (two marriages were performed in Kantunilkín in November 2011, annulled by the governor in April 2012, and reinstated on 3 May 2012 once the state conceded its Civil Code sets no gender requirement), and the state congress legalized adoption by same-sex couples in August 2022. The page records Quintana Roo among the states that enacted legal gender recognition in 2020 and that banned conversion practices on 15 December 2023, and lists the Quintana Roo penal code among hate-crime laws punishing crimes motivated by sexual orientation or gender. It also notes the state ratified the 2011 federal constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination and that Cancún is among Mexico's principal gay-tourism destinations.

sources.title: Quintana Roo y Morelos prohíben las terapias de conversión - Tribuna de la Bahía
sources.claim: Local reporting (Tribuna de la Bahía, 15 December 2023) on the Quintana Roo congress joining Morelos in banning conversion practices: both legislatures approved initiatives prohibiting and sanctioning 'Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual e Identidad de Género' (ECOSIG), commonly called conversion therapies, with penalties of two to six years in prison and fines of 1,000 to 2,000 times the daily UMA (measurement and updating unit) value for those who carry out such practices. This pins the December 2023 reform to a concrete date and gives the sanction levels in force across the state, including tourist corridors such as Cancún and the Riviera Maya.

records.name: Johor
records.current_summary:
Johor operates within the national framework without documented local divergence: same-sex conduct is criminalised with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping, there is no legal gender recognition, and public-morality offences are enforced through the state's religious authorities — the channel international monitoring documents as driving state-backed discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia.

No protective or tolerant regime specific to this state is on record. A visitor's exposure here is the national baseline, enforced locally.

sources.claim: Malaysia country profile (Human Dignity Trust, last updated 16 December 2025) — the national-framework source the record's baseline rests on — with Johor-specific content: in November 2023 the Johor government announced plans to establish conversion-therapy centres to "rehabilitate" LGBT people, the record's one documented local divergence beyond the national baseline. The framework applied locally: Penal Code sections 377A-377D criminalise same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment with whipping for both men and women, Sharia enactments prohibit cross-dressing and "males posing as females", same-sex intimacy is also criminalised by state Sharia laws applying to Muslims, and at least 1,733 people had attended "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021 under a crackdown ongoing since the 2018 election.

National-framework HRW/Justice for Sisters report release (10 August 2022) supporting the record's claim that the national baseline applies unchanged in Johor and is enforced through state religious authorities: the federal penal code punishes oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison, Sharia codes in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity, state-conducted investigations covered Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah, and a crackdown on the LGBT community has run since the 2018 election. No Johor-specific incident appears in this source; the record's local finding (Johor's 2023 conversion-therapy-centre plans) is covered by the paired Human Dignity Trust profile.

records.name: Malacca
records.current_summary:
Malacca enforces the national framework with no documented local mitigation: same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 20 years and whipping), there is no legal gender recognition, and public-morality policing runs through the state's religious authority — the agency type international monitoring identifies as the driver of state-backed discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia.

The heritage-tourism setting offers no recorded protection; visible gender nonconformity is exposed to that religious enforcement.

sources.claim: National-framework source (applies country-wide, including the state of Malacca): the Human Dignity Trust Malaysia country profile (last updated 2024) reports the Federal Penal Code 1936 ss.377A/377B criminalise same-sex sexual activity with a maximum penalty of twenty years’ imprisonment and whipping, and s.377D “outrages on decency” criminalises gross indecency in terms that can be used to target transgender people; state Sharia enactments additionally criminalise “cross-dressing” for Muslims. It records evidence of the law being enforced in recent years, a crackdown on the LGBT community since the 2018 election, a high-profile 2021 case of a prominent transgender woman fleeing the country following threats of arrest, and consistent reports of discrimination and violence with transgender people particularly vulnerable to physical and verbal abuse.

National-framework source (applies country-wide; no Malacca-specific breakdown): HRW report (published 10 Aug 2022 with Justice for Sisters) documents government-sponsored discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia, citing the federal penal code punishing oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison and Sharia law codes in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya that typically criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity. It details a hostile official climate — “rehabilitation” and conversion programs, officials shutting down events, and the 2021 prosecution of transgender woman Nur Sajat in western Selangor — and concludes pervasive antipathy toward sexual and gender diversity influences law enforcement, judicial outcomes, family behavior, and public discourse.

records.name: Abuja Federal Capital Territory
records.current_summary: Worse than national: the killing of the territory's most publicly visible trans person, followed by a refusal to investigate. On 8 August 2024 a 33-year-old transgender woman with a large TikTok following ('Abuja Area Mama') was found beaten and bruised beside the Katampe-Mabushi Expressway hours after posting a routine video, having previously expressed fear for her life; a human-rights group has since sued the federal government and the police for failing to investigate, seeking a court order compelling investigation and prosecution after multiple petitions were ignored — which qualifies the killing under the state-failure test rather than leaving it a lone incident. Reporting on the capital's queer scene documents threats and raids alongside informal community organising. The national framework applies here unchanged: same-sex conduct criminalised with up to 14 years' imprisonment, with dating-app 'kito' gangs a nationwide pattern; the UK's foreign office warned LGBT travellers in August 2026 of arrest, violence, attacks and blackmail risks. Scored relative to the national score (0.08) for Nigeria.

sources.claim: Region-specific: BBC News (article dated 9 Aug 2024) reports the beaten, bruised body of 33-year-old transgender TikToker “Abuja Area Mama” was found along the Katampe-Mabushi expressway in the Banex/Wuse II area of Abuja on Thursday 8 August 2024, hours after she posted a final video, having previously expressed fear for her life; a police statement described the victim as “a man fully dressed in female clothing with no means of identification”. Abuja police chief Benneth Igweh ordered a “thorough and discreet” investigation, and the article notes that although Nigerian laws guarantee freedom from discrimination, mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in northern states.

Region-specific: The Dial (Issue 25) reports police found Area Mama dead on an Abuja highway hours after her last video; Abuja police’s preliminary statement described her as “a man fully dressed in female clothing”, and six months later no suspects had been charged despite a promised “thorough and discreet” investigation. It details the legal floor her killers faced — the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforcing colonial-era laws criminalising same-sex activity as “carnal knowledge against the order of nature” punishable by up to 14 years’ imprisonment, bans on same-sex marriage and civil unions, gay organisations and public LGBTQ+ expression, death-by-stoning risk under northern Sharia law, no legal route to change gender, and cross-dressing bans under Sharia in the north and in the Nigerian military — and records a nearly 6,000-signature petition demanding investigation of her murder as a hate crime.

National-framework source (applies country-wide; no Abuja-specific breakdown): Sahara Reporters (19 Aug 2026) reports the United Kingdom's foreign office warned LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of the risk of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation. The advisory states same-sex sexual activity is illegal and can attract lengthy prison sentences, that some northern states operating under Sharia law can impose the death penalty, and that the law also extends to people who help arrange or conduct same-sex marriages and criminalises activities involving gay groups and organisations; breaching curfews or movement restrictions could expose travellers to arrest and detention.

freshness_all.fact: Current (19 Aug 2026): UK advisory cites attacks, 14-year SSMPA terms and sharia death-penalty risk; FCT remains federal enforcement hub.
The Aug 2024 Abuja death of a trans creator remains a live enforcement/climate marker; nothing superseding found.

records.name: Lima
records.current_summary:
Lima concentrates the country's sharpest documented lethality and its newest legal restriction. An LGBTI human-rights observatory at a national university counted 54 LGBTI+ murders for 2020–2023, with trans women the most affected, amid rising hate crimes. In 2025 the national congress — sitting and operating out of the capital — approved a norm against trans people's use of public bathrooms (committee vote February 2025; floor vote April 2025), which a national human-rights institute published an analysis calling legalised discrimination with direct consequences for access to public space.

For a trans visitor, the capital is therefore where both mechanisms bite: the bathroom-restriction norm is national policy administered here, and the murder pattern shows the violence risk when prosecutions are rare and official statistics thin.
records.current_outOfScope: Lima Centro concentrates the highest national frequency of reported crimes overall (10.0%; eleven fiscal districts hold 62%) — general crime, not trans-specific; general crime and political instability affect all travellers.

sources.claim: National-framework source (binds Lima as national policy): Infobae (20 Feb 2025) reports the Congress Women and Family Commission unanimously approved the Muñante initiative barring trans people from public bathrooms of the sex not matching their biological sex at birth, stating the text also bars “ambiguous” bathroom signage of the kind the international airport Jorge Chávez had placed (“for all persons with female identity” / “male identity”) and that the norm still required plenary backing. LGBTIQ activist Gianna Camacho is quoted calling the measure discriminatory and describing how enforcement would reduce to security staff demanding ID (DNI) based on their own judgment of whether a woman entering is trans.

National-framework source (the norm is national policy, enacted by the congress that sits and operates in Lima): IDEHPUCP analysis (15 Apr 2025, Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte) reports the Congress plenary on Wednesday 2 April 2025 approved, exempt from a second vote, the fused bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR; article 5 of the text prohibits entry to and use of public sanitary facilities by any person whose biological sex does not match the sex for which the facility is designated, with listed exceptions. The authors call the rule direct legislation that conditions basic rights on a “biological sex”, a violation of the equality and non-discrimination principle, and note trans people, though framed as aggressors, are more often victims of violence and discrimination.

National-framework source (observatory counts include Lima): Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024) reports the TLGBI Rights Observatory annual report recorded 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 reports of rights violations between 2020 and 2023, more than half of the dead being trans women (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian; 2023 saw the most homicides (19) and no suspects were identified in 26 of the 54 killings. It recounts the 12 Feb 2023 kidnapping of transgender sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano (31) from jirón Chancay in central Lima by the “Los Gallegos” extortion gang, who killed her with roughly 30 gunshots, and flags state inaction: no official system records victims’ sexual orientation and hate crimes go unsanctioned.

records.name: Malta
records.current_summary:
Malta is among the safest countries in the world for transgender visitors. It has ranked first in Europe for LGBTI legal rights every year since 2015: gender identity and expression are protected from discrimination in law, legal gender recognition works by self-determination, and "X" gender markers are available on passports. Conversion therapy is banned and the constitution guarantees LGBTI equality.

Malta records one of the lowest rates of physical or sexual victimisation of LGBTIQ+ people in the EU, and the national police force has adopted hate-crime procedures for SOGIE incidents. The US State Department describes Malta as a safe environment for foreign LGBT travellers, and no government travel advisory flags trans-specific concerns.

Residual risks are minor: non-physical harassment (including online) is more common than violence but tends to be under-reported, and — in the unlikely event of arrest — prison practice has been found to lag the country's progressive law, with transgender inmates reporting gaps in healthcare and placement procedures.
records.current_localsOnly: The self-determination LGR regime and passport X markers are resident-facing administrative law; the prison healthcare/placement gaps concern resident inmates.
records.current_outOfScope: Petty crime around nightclubs and tourist spots, and general European terrorism guidance, are ordinary travel risks that affect everyone.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map country page for Malta with the compliance breakdown across asylum, civil-society space, intersex bodily integrity, legal gender recognition, hate crime/hate speech and equality-body categories, scored per category on the map's red-to-green scale.

Equaldex data for Malta: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change with no restrictions, nonbinary recognised, hate-crime protections cover SOGI, discrimination illegal, full ban on intersex infant surgery, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. 84% rate it a 'good place' for gay people; but Maltese rank #1 of 30 EU regions for hiding being LGBTIQ at work.

Legal status: same-sex conduct legal since 29 January 1973; civil unions since 2014 and same-sex marriage since 2017; gender change without surgery; full adoption since 2014; open military service; discrimination protections cover sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics.

Academic chapter (Routledge Companion to Gender and Crime, 2025, Mary Grace Vella): Malta records one of the lowest SOGIE physical/sexual victimisation rates in the EU27, yet LGBTIQ+ people still report a higher share of harassment and online hatred, and reporting of violence to the Malta Police Force remains significantly low despite institutional reforms.

University of Malta dissertation (Oriana Vidal, 2024): four interviews with current/former transgender inmates at the Correctional Service Agency (25-year cohort) found healthcare, legislative and knowledge gaps plus post-release problems, with CSA practice out of sync with national gender-identity legislation — institutional lag beneath the strong statute book.

ICJ (30 July 2025): ICJ and partners filed observations in M.S. v. Malta at the ECtHR — an LGBTI asylum seeker detained on arrival in Malta in April 2023 received a return decision and removal order to Bangladesh in May 2024; submissions raise ECHR Articles 3/5/13 (non-refoulement, detention conditions, individualised assessment before detention). Direct evidence of how LGBTI arrivals are treated at Maltese borders.

MaltaToday (15 April 2014): parliament approved the constitutional amendment naming gender identity — Malta the first European state to do so — and introduced civil unions in the same sitting; Transgender Europe was among the first NGOs to applaud gender identity as a protected ground in the highest legal text.

records.name: Iceland
records.current_summary:
Iceland is one of the safest countries in the world for transgender visitors. The 2019 Gender Autonomy Act allows self-defined gender registration without diagnosis or surgery, non-binary people can use an "X" marker, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity and expression is banned in services and employment. General crime rates are very low.

Local travel businesses actively accommodate trans visitors: a dedicated traveller guide from Pink Iceland reports that most Reykjavík-area swimming pools offer private or gender-neutral changing rooms, that using binary changing rooms is legal and common, and that trans visitors generally "shouldn't have to be worried about your safety". Emergency services maintain dedicated guidance for queer victims of abuse and hate crime.

Residual risks are small: potential hate-crime reports have risen in recent years (from very low absolute levels), Iceland's hate-crime law works through sentencing aggravation rather than a standalone offence, and occasional misgendering — usually unintentional — still occurs.
records.current_localsOnly: The 2019 Gender Autonomy Act's self-defined registration and X marker are resident-facing processes.
records.current_outOfScope: Iceland's principal hazards are natural (weather, road conditions, geothermal and volcanic areas) and affect all travellers equally.

sources.claim: thin: no usable finding

Outright International (last update 12 Mar 2026): Iceland at-a-glance — same-sex relations legal nationwide for men and women, legal gender recognition possible, LGBTI organisations able to register; progressive laws with acknowledged gaps remain.

Equaldex data for Iceland: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change with no restrictions, nonbinary recognised, hate-crime protections cover SOGI, discrimination illegal, full ban on intersex infant surgery, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. Ranked #1 of 121 regions for 'good place' for gay and lesbian people (93%).

112.is national emergency guidance: hate-crime explainer — umbrella term for offences committed from prejudice/hatred, with victims/perpetrators, hate-speech and reporting sections (Iceland).
112.is: abuse against queer people — notes queer people are more likely to be victims of violence, with guidance and reporting routes via 112.

Iceland Review: police-recorded potential hate crimes rose — 16 cases in 2023 (triple the prior year), 11 in 2024, 7 already in the current year; queer rights group Samtökin 78 calls for stronger hate-crime legislation as incidents climb.
GOV.UK Iceland travel advice: same-sex sexual activity legal and same-sex relationships recognised in law; dedicated LGBT+ traveller advice linked — safety assessment for British visitors.
Ísland.is: Equality Complaints Committee — the official equality/discrimination complaints mechanism for Iceland (institutional redress route).

Reykjavík Grapevine (2 Aug 2019): history of Icelandic trans-law reform — the earlier law was among Europe's most progressive, replaced by a newer self-determination process; activists (incl. Trans Ísland chair) map remaining challenges.
